newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Spy chief says foreigners try to subvert S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Spy chief says foreigners try to subvert S.Africa.

text.p: South Africa's spy chief said on Wednesday foreign secret agents were flooding into the country and some of them appeared bent on subverting President Nelson Mandela's government.

Sizakele Sigxashe, director-general of the National Intelligence Agency (NIA), told reporters that the number of foreign spies operating in South Africa had doubled or trebled since democratic elections in April 1994.
"With the coming in of the present dispensation, a lot of embassies have opened," he said.
"They have declared officials of security agencies, but at the same time we have got a bigger number which are not declared. We have lots and lots of them, they are under watch."
Asked what foreign countries aimed to achieve through espionage in South Africa, Sigxashe said:
"Some of them, they could be also trying to...subvert the country to go back to what it was before. There are new developments which are indicating things of that nature.
"But we are still investigating, it is difficult to talk about that. It is of grave concern."
Sigxashe said many foreign spy agencies had moved their African listening posts to South Africa from elsewhere on the continent since 1994.

They were interested in economic and technological intelligence and some took a particular interest in arms programmes such as the secret chemical warfare project that has come to light in a recent court hearing.
Sigxashe predicted "very startling things" were yet to emerge in the case of Wouter Basson, a former army officer who played a leading role in South African chemical warfare research.

He was arrested earlier this year on drug smuggling charges. Evidence during his bail hearing suggested that South Africa developed an offensive capacity in chemical and biological warfare, not just the defensive measures the country has previously acknowledged.
"It was advanced technology," Sigxashe said, adding that the United States and Britain were keen to discover the extent of the programme and to make sure the technology did not reach other countries.

One of Sigxashe's predecessors has said foreign agents in South Africa had tried to recruit scientists who worked on the country's nuclear warfare programme. South Africa built six warheads in the 1980s but has since dismantled them.
